title: “EVERYTHING IS PERMISSIBLE”—THE DANGEROUS LIE THAT ALMOST DESTROYED THE CORINTHIAN CHURCH
paragraphs: “EVERYTHING IS PERMISSIBLE”—THE DANGEROUS LIE THAT ALMOST DESTROYED THE CORINTHIAN CHURCH
They believed grace gave them freedom to do whatever they wanted. Paul confronted them with a terrifying question: What if the very thing you call freedom has already made you its slave?
There is a kind of prison that does not have bars.
Its doors are wide open. Its prisoners can go wherever they want. They laugh, worship, post Bible verses, attend church, and tell everyone they are doing just fine.
But when nobody is watching, something else is in control.
An appetite they cannot silence.
A relationship they know they should leave.
A secret they keep promising God they will surrender.
A habit they defend in public but regret in private.
And perhaps the most dangerous part?
They have learned how to use the language of freedom to justify the very thing that is destroying them.
“God knows my heart.”
“I'm under grace, not the law.”
“Nobody is perfect.”
“It's my body. It's my life.”
“As long as I believe in Jesus, what difference does it make?”
If any of those words sound familiar, stay with me.
Because nearly two thousand years ago, the apostle Paul confronted a church that had become dangerously comfortable with this kind of thinking.
And what he wrote was not merely a correction for ancient Corinth.
It is a mirror for the modern Christian.
A mirror that may expose something we have spent years refusing to see.
The most frightening bondage is the one you have convinced yourself is freedom.

The city of Corinth was wealthy, influential, religiously diverse, and notorious for its moral temptations. It was a major commercial center where competing philosophies, social ambitions, and sexual practices shaped everyday life.
And right in the middle of that complicated city, God had established a church.
Real believers.
People who had heard the Gospel, believed in Jesus Christ, and been brought out of their former ways of life.
Yet something was going terribly wrong.
The culture surrounding them was beginning to influence the way some of them understood Christian freedom.
They had received the message of grace, but some appeared to be using freedom as an excuse for indulgence.
Paul confronted their reasoning with words that remain painfully relevant:
“All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any.” — 1 Corinthians 6:12, KJV
Read that last sentence again.
“I will not be brought under the power of any.”
That is where the comfortable Christian life suddenly becomes uncomfortable.
Because Paul was not simply asking whether someone could do something.
He was asking what that thing was doing to them.
Was it helping them follow Christ?
Was it building them up?
Or was it quietly becoming their master?
In the original Greek, the phrase translated “All things are lawful” is:
Πάντα μοι ἔξεστιν — Panta moi exestin.
It means, in context, “All things are permissible for me” or “All things are lawful for me.”

Many biblical interpreters understand Paul to be repeating a slogan used by some Corinthians and then correcting its misuse. The text does not explicitly identify the original speaker, so we should be careful not to claim more than Scripture tells us.
But Paul's response is unmistakable.
ἀλλ᾽ οὐ πάντα συμφέρει — all’ ou panta sympherei.
“But not all things are beneficial.”
The Greek verb sympherei carries the idea of something being advantageous, profitable, or beneficial.
In other words, even when an action is not inherently forbidden, that does not automatically make it spiritually wise.
Then Paul goes deeper.
ἀλλ᾽ οὐκ ἐγὼ ἐξουσιασθήσομαι ὑπό τινος — all’ ouk egō exousiasthēsomai hypo tinos.
“But I will not be mastered by anything.”
The verb exousiasthēsomai comes from a Greek word family associated with authority or power. Here, Paul speaks of being brought under another's control.
Notice the force of his argument.
The Corinthians spoke about what they had permission to do.
Paul spoke about what had power over them.
They were concerned with their rights.
Paul was concerned with their spiritual freedom.
And there is a world of difference between those two things.
Because you can have permission to enjoy something and still become enslaved to it.
You can possess something without being controlled by it.
You can participate in something without allowing it to become your identity.
But when you cannot say no anymore, you need to ask whether you are still the one making the decisions.
That question becomes even more serious when we remember what Paul was actually addressing.
He was not writing a vague motivational speech about productivity, self-discipline, or breaking bad habits.
He was confronting sexual immorality and a distorted understanding of the human body.
The next verse says:
“Meats for the belly, and the belly for meats: but God shall destroy both it and them. Now the body is not for fornication, but for the Lord; and the Lord for the body.” — 1 Corinthians 6:13, KJV
The Corinthians apparently had a way of reasoning about bodily appetites that treated sexual desire as though it were simply another physical need.
Food is for the stomach.
The stomach is for food.
So why should satisfying sexual appetite be any different?
Paul refused that comparison.
Food and sexual intimacy are not morally interchangeable simply because both involve the body.
The human body is not an insignificant container that the soul can use however it pleases.
“The body is not for fornication, but for the Lord; and the Lord for the body.”
The Greek word translated “fornication” is porneia (πορνεία), a broad biblical term for sexual immorality.
Paul's concern was not that the body was evil.
Quite the opposite.
The body mattered so much that he reminded believers of its relationship to Jesus Christ.
And then, in verse 14, he wrote something that should change the way every Christian thinks about the physical life:
“And God hath both raised up the Lord, and will also raise up us by his own power.” — 1 Corinthians 6:14, KJV
Do you see it?
The Christian hope is not escape from the body as though the body were worthless.
It is resurrection.
Jesus Christ rose bodily from the dead, and believers have the promise of resurrection through Him.
Your body matters because God's redemptive purpose includes it.
Your choices matter because you belong to Christ.
Your sexuality matters because the Lord who redeemed you is also the Lord who calls you to holiness.
And that is where this ancient letter becomes painfully personal.
Because many of us have become very skilled at asking the wrong question.
We ask, “How far can I go before it becomes sin?”
Instead of, “How can I honor Jesus with my life?”
We ask, “Where does the Bible specifically forbid this?”
Instead of, “Is this drawing my heart closer to Christ?”
We ask, “Can I still be saved if I keep doing this?”
Instead of, “Why am I fighting so hard to keep something that is pulling me away from the One who saved me?”
Those are not the same questions.
And the difference matters.
Christian freedom was never intended to become an excuse for making peace with sin.
Paul would later write:
Freedom in Christ is real.
But it is not freedom from Christ's authority.
It is freedom from sin's dominion so that we may belong to Him and walk in love.
And perhaps that is the truth some of us have been avoiding.
We want Jesus to forgive us.
But we resist when He begins changing us.
We want the comfort of His promises.
But we struggle with the demands of discipleship.
We want the cross to remove our guilt.
But sometimes we hesitate to let it confront our idols.
And still, Jesus does not stop calling us.
Not because sin is harmless.
Not because repentance is optional.
But because His grace is greater than the darkness we are afraid to surrender.
Think about the person reading this at two in the morning.
The one who has just fallen into the same sin they promised God they would never repeat.
Their Bible is nearby.
Their phone is still in their hand.
They know what happened.
They know the excuses.
They know the shame that follows.
And they are tired.
Tired of asking forgiveness.
Tired of starting over.
Tired of feeling spiritually divided.
Tired of appearing strong in church while privately feeling defeated.
Maybe that person is you.
Maybe you have begun to wonder whether genuine transformation is even possible.
Listen carefully.
Your repeated struggle is not evidence that Jesus has run out of mercy. But His mercy is never permission to surrender yourself to the sin He came to save you from.
That distinction could change your life.
Because the Gospel does not tell you to pretend your sin is small.
It tells you that Christ is a sufficient Savior.
The Gospel does not say your actions are meaningless.
It announces that forgiveness and a new life are possible through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
And the Gospel does not leave the believer alone to manufacture holiness through willpower.
God gives His Spirit to those who belong to Christ.
Paul had already reminded these same Corinthians of the lives some of them once lived.
In 1 Corinthians 6:9–10, he warned that those characterized by persistent unrighteousness would not inherit the kingdom of God.
He did not soften the seriousness of sin.
He did not redefine holiness to make the surrounding culture comfortable.
But then came one of the most beautiful sentences in the entire letter.
“And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.” — 1 Corinthians 6:11, KJV
And such were some of you.
Were.
Not because their past never happened.
Not because their wounds instantly disappeared.
Not because every temptation vanished overnight.
But because Jesus Christ had changed their standing before God and brought them into a new life.
They were washed.
They were sanctified.
They were justified.
Those words are not decorations for a religious speech.
They describe the astonishing work of God's grace.
The Greek word translated “washed” is apelousasthe (ἀπελούσασθε), referring here to cleansing.
The word translated “sanctified” is hēgiasthēte (ἡγιάσθητε), describing being made holy or set apart.
The word translated “justified” is edikaiōthēte (ἐδικαιώθητε), speaking of being declared righteous.
And Paul places these realities in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
This is not a story about people rescuing themselves through moral perfection.
It is a story about sinners receiving the grace of God through Jesus Christ.
That is why the phrase “And such were some of you” carries so much hope.
Your past can be real without remaining your identity.
Your sin can be serious without being beyond Christ's power to forgive.
Your repentance can be painful without being pointless.
Your transformation can be ongoing without being imaginary.
And your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
From scandal to grace. Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But we must understand what that means.
Jesus does not rewrite our story by pretending that evil was good.
He does not call darkness light.
He does not erase the need for repentance.
He rewrites our story through redemption.
Through the cross.
Through the empty tomb.
Through forgiveness that we could never earn.
Through the Spirit who continues transforming those who belong to Him.
And sometimes that transformation begins with a deeply uncomfortable admission.
“Lord, I have been calling something freedom when it has actually been controlling me.”
That confession may be the beginning of a different kind of life.
Perhaps you need to end a relationship that continually draws you into sexual sin.
Perhaps you need to confess a hidden addiction to a trustworthy, mature Christian who can help you pursue accountability.
Perhaps you need to stop treating pornography as harmless entertainment.
Perhaps you need to confront dishonesty, pride, bitterness, or a consuming desire for approval.
Perhaps you have allowed social media, money, pleasure, or other people's opinions to exercise authority over your heart.
Not every strong desire is sinful.
Not every pleasure is forbidden.
And not every difficult habit is evidence of spiritual rebellion.
But anything that begins ruling your life deserves serious examination before God.
The issue is not whether you can construct an argument defending it.
The issue is whether you can honestly bring it before Jesus.
Paul's words expose something modern Christianity desperately needs to remember.
A person can win an argument about personal freedom and still lose the battle for self-control.
That is why 1 Corinthians 6:12 is not a command to live in fear of everything enjoyable.
It is a call to refuse slavery to anything that competes with Christ's rightful lordship.
And Paul's argument reaches its climax a few verses later.

“What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's.” — 1 Corinthians 6:19–20, KJV
Ye are not your own.
Those words confront the individualism of every generation.
The Christian does not belong to Christ because God has taken away human dignity.
The Christian belongs to Christ because Jesus has redeemed us at immeasurable cost.
And the price was not money.
It was His sacrificial death.
The sinless Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
He was crucified.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
This is why the call to holiness cannot be separated from the Gospel.
We do not pursue holiness to purchase salvation.
We pursue holiness because the Savior who purchased our redemption is worthy of our lives.
Grace is not the reward for becoming perfect.
Grace is God's undeserved favor in Christ, which teaches and transforms those who receive it.
As Titus 2:11–12 teaches, the grace of God trains believers to renounce ungodliness and live godly lives.
Real grace does more than comfort the guilty conscience.
It begins changing the surrendered heart.
And no, that does not mean every Christian will experience instant victory over every temptation.
Some battles require years of prayer, wise counsel, accountability, practical boundaries, and patient growth.
Some wounds need careful attention.
Some habits require serious intervention.
But none of that makes repentance meaningless.
The believer who falls must not be encouraged to despair.
Nor should they be encouraged to make peace with the fall.
First John 1:9 reminds us that God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse those who confess their sins.
And Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
No condemnation in Christ does not mean no conviction.
It means that those who belong to Jesus need not flee from Him in hopelessness when His truth exposes their sin.
They can come into the light.
They can confess.
They can repent.
They can receive mercy.
They can continue learning to walk in obedience.
And if you are reading this with tears in your eyes because something has finally been exposed, please hear this.
You do not have to impress Jesus with a performance of spiritual strength.
Come to Him truthfully.
Tell Him where you are struggling.
Tell Him what you have been hiding.
Tell Him where you have confused liberty with license.
Ask Him to forgive you.
Ask Him to change you.
Then take the next faithful step.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you feel spiritually impressive.
Today.
Maybe that means opening your Bible again.
Maybe it means deleting something that repeatedly leads you into temptation.
Maybe it means reaching out to a pastor, mentor, or mature believer instead of fighting alone.
Maybe it means making restitution for a wrong.
Maybe it means choosing honesty when hiding would be easier.
The next step may seem small.
But obedience does not become insignificant simply because nobody applauds it.
And the Lord sees the heart that turns toward Him.
There is something else worth remembering.
Paul did not write this letter to a church filled with people who had never failed.
He wrote to a deeply troubled congregation.
There were divisions.
Pride.
Confusion.
Moral compromise.
Misunderstandings about spiritual gifts.
Disorder in worship.
Even serious questions about the resurrection.
Yet Paul continued instructing them in the truth of Christ.
He confronted their sin because their lives mattered.
He corrected their thinking because the Gospel mattered.
He called them to holiness because their bodies and souls belonged to the Lord.
And through Scripture, that correction still speaks to us.
Not every choice that feels liberating leads to freedom.
Not every desire deserves obedience.
Not every cultural permission carries God's approval.
Not everything you can do is something you should do.
And not everything that promises satisfaction can give you peace.
The question is no longer simply, “Am I allowed?”
The question is, “Does this honor the Jesus who gave His life for me?”
That question reaches far beyond sexual ethics.
It reaches into the words we speak to our spouses.
The way we treat our children.
The entertainment we consume.
The money we spend.
The grudges we protect.
The private thoughts we nurture.
The way we use our influence.
The people we exploit.
The truth we avoid.
The sacrifices we refuse to make.
And even the way we handle the blessings God has entrusted to us.
Because a life redeemed by Christ is not divided into sacred Sundays and unrelated weekdays.
Jesus is Lord over all of it.
And this is where our faith must move beyond agreement into action.
If this message has confronted you, do not let it become another article you read, appreciated, and forgot.
Bring the truth before God.
Sit with the question Paul raises.
What has been exercising authority over you?
What have you defended simply because you did not want to surrender it?
What would change if honoring Christ became more important than protecting your comfort?
You do not need to publish the details of your private struggles for strangers to examine.
But you can take a meaningful step toward honesty.
Someone reading may desperately need to know that change through Christ is possible.
There is no shame in asking fellow believers to pray for you.
There is strength in bringing struggles into the light with wisdom and discernment.
And there is beauty in reminding one another that our hope is not in ourselves, but in Jesus Christ.
Perhaps you know someone who needs this message.
A friend who has slowly drifted from the faith.
A young believer surrounded by confusing ideas about freedom.
A family member who has mistaken God's patience for indifference.
A Christian who feels trapped in a cycle of compromise.
Or someone who does not yet know Jesus but has discovered that the world's promises of freedom have left them empty.
Not to shame anyone.
Not to appear more righteous than others.
But because biblical truth deserves to travel beyond the people who already agree with it.
Invite your friends, family, struggling believers, seekers, and even those who do not yet believe to join us as we keep pointing people to Jesus Christ.
But I also want to speak to those who believe this work is worth sustaining.

Every article we publish, every biblical truth we share, and every resource we make available is part of a larger mission: helping people encounter the Gospel and grow in their understanding of God's Word.
These resources are intended to encourage Bible study, spiritual maturity, and a closer walk with the Lord.
And keeping this work moving forward requires real effort, time, resources, and ongoing support.
Not because God requires you to support this particular ministry to prove your faith.
And certainly not because a monthly payment can purchase His favor.
Salvation is God's gift through Jesus Christ, not a benefit anyone can buy.
But Scripture does teach that generosity can be an expression of love, gratitude, and partnership in the work of the Gospel.
In Philippians 4:15–17, Paul spoke appreciatively of believers who shared in supporting his ministry, while emphasizing the spiritual fruit of their generosity.
And 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That is the spirit in which I invite you to participate.
These are small ways we can say thank you to those who choose to walk alongside this mission.
Someone in your circle may never visit a Christian page on their own.
But they may stop to read something you share.
They may recognize themselves in Paul's warning.
They may open their Bible.
They may ask for prayer.
They may begin to understand the Gospel.
And perhaps, through that encounter with God's Word, they may be drawn toward Jesus Christ.
We cannot manufacture spiritual transformation.
Only God can change a heart.
But we can faithfully proclaim the truth, serve others in love, and trust Him with the results.
And now, before you leave, return with me to the words that started everything.
“All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient.”
Paul was not trying to steal joy from the Corinthians.
He was showing them that freedom without wisdom can become another form of slavery.
That the body belongs to the Lord.
That holiness matters.
That grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
And that Jesus Christ is worthy of more than a carefully managed portion of our lives.
Maybe the thing you have been defending is the very thing God is calling you to surrender.
Maybe the freedom you have been searching for will not be found in another excuse, another distraction, or another promise to try harder.
Maybe it begins with coming honestly to the Savior who died and rose again.
Not hiding.
Not bargaining.
Not pretending.
Just surrendering.

“Lord Jesus, I have called some things freedom that have only brought me further into bondage. Forgive me for the ways I have misused Your grace. Teach me to honor You with my body, my thoughts, my choices, and my life. Help me turn away from sin and walk in the freedom You have given through Your death and resurrection. Give me the courage to obey, the humility to seek help, and the faith to trust Your Word above my desires. I belong to You. In Jesus' name, amen.”
And if that prayer reflects what is happening in your heart, do not leave this moment behind without responding.
Let it be a simple confession of faith and surrender, not a performance for others.
But above all, remember this.
The Gospel is not the story of how good people earned God's acceptance.
It is the story of how Jesus Christ came to save sinners, reconcile them to God, and make them new.
Corinth had its scandals.
We have ours.
Corinth had its compromises.
We have ours.
But the same risen Christ proclaimed by Paul remains the only Savior who can forgive our sins, break sin's dominion, and bring us into newness of life.
And that is why your story does not have to end where your shame began.
The chains you once called freedom do not have to be the chains you carry into tomorrow.
